name: Voltage-rated rubber insulating gloves
summary: Rubber gloves made and electrically tested to insulate a trained worker's hands up to a stated voltage, worn with leather protectors over them.
uses: Shock protection up to the class's maximum use voltage, but only if in date, inspected and air-tested that day, and worn with protectors (OSHA 1910.137)
Not for untrained people: only qualified, trained workers may work on live parts; everyone else switches off and proves dead first (OSHA 1910.333, IHSA LIVE WORK)
Class 00 and 0 are for low voltage up to 500 or 1,000 V AC; classes 1 to 4 are for higher voltage, from 7,500 up to 36,000 V AC (OSHA 1910.137)
Leather protectors over the rubber guard it against mechanical damage and heat; the leather gives no electrical protection itself (ASTM F696)
They protect the hands only; rubber sleeves are needed if the arms can come near live parts (OSHA ETOOL GLOVES)
identify: Thick rubber gauntlets, often 11 or 14 inches (280 or 360 mm) long; some have a different colour inside and out so cuts show up (HONEYWELL CLASS 0). US and Canada: ASTM D120 gloves, six classes (ASTM D120, E-HAZARD). The class is marked on the cuff (OSHA 1910.137) on a coloured label: 00 beige, max use 500 V AC / 750 V DC; 0 red, 1,000 / 1,500; 1 white, 7,500 / 11,250; 2 yellow, 17,000 / 25,500; 3 green, 26,500 / 39,750; 4 orange, 36,000 / 54,000 (OSHA 1910.137 for AC, PNNL GLOVE CHECKLIST for DC and colours). Type I is not ozone-resistant, Type II is (OSHA 1910.137). Europe: EN or IEC 60903, the same classes and voltages, colour labels optional, with letters A acid, H oil, Z ozone, R all three, C extreme cold (SATRA EN 60903). Gloves are stamped with a test or issue date (PNNL GLOVE CHECKLIST). Fakes: gloves sold online with a lightning bolt or a 'proof voltage test' claim, but no named standard and class marking, prove nothing; the bolt is only a hazard warning (E-HAZARD). Arc-rated work gloves give no shock protection (E-HAZARD). Leather protectors are not insulating gloves (ASTM F696). The glove's own colour is not the class; the same class comes in several colours (HONEYWELL CLASS 0).
test: Every day before use, inspect inside and out. Any hole, tear, puncture, cut, ozone cracking, embedded object, or swelling, softening, hardening or stickiness puts the glove out of service (OSHA 1910.137). Air test: roll the cuff to trap air or use an inflator, then squeeze, listen and feel for leaks on both sides (PNNL GLOVE CHECKLIST, E-HAZARD). Check the stamped date: in the US gloves are electrically retested before first issue and every 6 months, and OSHA lets gloves tested but never issued go into service within 12 months, but PNNL counts 6 months from the stamped date even on the shelf; treat 6 as the limit (OSHA 1910.137, PNNL GLOVE CHECKLIST); in Ontario, gloves rated above 5,000 V AC are retested every 3 months in service (IHSA LIVE WORK). OSHA requires both the daily air test and the periodic electrical retest (OSHA 1910.137). Inspect protectors for holes, popped seams, oil and embedded metal, and keep at least this gap between the protector cuff and the rubber cuff: 13 mm for class 00 and 0, 25 mm class 1, 51 mm class 2, 76 mm class 3, 102 mm class 4 (PNNL GLOVE CHECKLIST). Store unfolded, in a bag away from light, heat, damp and ozone, and not inside the protectors (OSHA ETOOL GLOVES, PNNL GLOVE CHECKLIST).

decay.note: The stamped electrical test lapses after 6 months (OSHA allows 12 for gloves tested but never issued; PNNL counts 6) and can't be redone without a test lab; the rubber then ages from ozone, light and heat, natural rubber fastest (OSHA 1910.137, PNNL GLOVE CHECKLIST, S+H SHELF LIFE).

improvise: There is no substitute. Only gloves marked with an ASTM D120 class and kept within their test date count as insulating (OSHA 1910.137): kitchen, chemical and nitrile gloves are not, and leather gloves are only the protector, with no electrical protection (ASTM F696). Count on none of them. Do this instead: treat every wire as live, switch off and isolate the supply, lock or tag it, and prove it dead with a tester before you touch anything, checking the tester works just before and after (required above 600 V, wise always). OSHA makes de-energizing the default and requires this test, which also catches backfeed (OSHA 1910.333). If you can't make it dead, leave it. Found insulating gloves that are out of date or have no test stamp have no rating you can count on: never use them for live work. Untrained people must never rely on them for live work, even in date (OSHA 1910.333, IHSA LIVE WORK).
